subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: I was concerned about that in connection with this question of extraterritoriality and whether this amendment in section 2 is not necessary to make it clear that section 3 has an extraterritorial effect. I think the minister will agree with me that we do not need any amendment as to extraterritoriality in that particular part of section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Which part of section 3?

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
I am referring to subsections 3 and 4 particularly. Subsection 3 of the present section 3 reads:
In any proceedings against a person for an offence under this section, the fact that he has been in communciation with, or attempted to communicate with, an agent of a foreign power, whether within or without Canada, shall be evidence that he has, for a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state, obtained or attempted to obtain information which is calculated to be or might be or is intended to be directly or indirectly useful to a foreign power.
It seems to me that section 2 of the bill .giving extraterritorial effect to the whole act is not necessary, but that is not the point I was about to make, unless the minister wishes to comment on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Is the point not this, that section 3 and the other section that my hon. friend read earlier-

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Section 13.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: -section 13(1) and section 3(3) are references in the act to the effect that certain circumstances will have certain effects, and in relation to what? In relation to an act. What act? An act committed in Canada, as the statute stands at the present time. It is only when we give extraterritorial effect to the act by the bill now before hon. members that we can utilize those sections to which my hon. friend1 has referred in a prosecution in Canada in respect of an offence which has been committed outside Canada. In other words, you cannot have any extraterritorial quality in an act unless you specifically provide it, and that is what we are doing in the present case. You must specify in the statute that the act of the accused will be an offence in spite of the fact that it took place outside Canadian territory.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
The point I am making is with respect to section 3 of the present act, but I am prepared to concede the validity of the -minister's argument that as to the other
[Mr. Garson.l
sections there is no such provision and therefore the amendment incorporated in the bill to give extraterritorial effect is necessary and desirable. It seems to me we now have it doubly sure in so far as section 3 is concerned. I wanted to ask the minister if he will concede-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will read subsection 3 of section 3 of the present act he will see that it says:
In any proceedings against a person for an offence under this section, the fact that he has been in communication with, or attempted to communicate with, an agent of a foreign power, whether within or without Canada . . .
As the act now stands, that refers to the agent of the foreign power. If the person within Canada has communicated or attempted to communicate with an agent of a foreign power outside Canada he will be guilty of the offence.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: That is a pretty narrow restriction on the wording which I do not think is quite justified when you read the words in their plain connotation. What I want to ask the minister is whether subsection 3 of section 3, with its present extraterritorial effect, would not be available to justify prosecution and obtain a conviction against known communists of the type to which the hon. member for Lake Centre referred, who go to these countries and obviously communicate with agents of foreign powers, and whose character, known conduct, and so on establish in accordance with the terms of the act that they are doing it for a purpose prejudicial- and in fact they are assumed to be by the wording of the section-to the safety of the state. I want to ask the minister whether, now that we have the extraterritorial effect given by the amendment, we will not be in a position to prosecute people who go behind the iron curtain and communicate with agents of foreign powers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: I am afraid I did not quite understand the hon. member.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: I am asking the minister whether we will now be in a position to prosecute known communists who go behind the iron curtain and communicate with agents of foreign powers. I am asking whether, with the extraterritorial effect being given to the whole act, we will not be able to prosecute such people under section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Yes, I think we shall certainly be able to do so, but subject of course to the fact that you have to apprehend them in Canada if they return here and you have to get evidence of what they did in the foreign country. Then you could prosecute them.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
I may be interpreting the words too widely, but what I am interested in now is subsection 2 of section 3. I am happy if it has the result I hope it has. That subsection reads:
On a prosecution under this section, it shall not be necessary to show that the accused person was guilty of any particular act tending to show a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state, and, notwithstanding that no such act is proved against him-
That is, no particular act.
-he may be convicted if, from the circumstances of the case, or his conduct, or his known character as proved, it appears that his purpose was a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state...
With the extraterritorial effect which the act will now have, and which I say it had before but which we agree it has now, I wonder whether those words are wide enough to justify prosecution against known communists-I will name one if you like, Tim Buck-who go behind the iron curtain and communicate intimately and at length with agents-I do not mean just citizens-of foreign powers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Let us look at the beginning of section 3. It reads:
3. (1) If any person for any purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state-
I shall omit (a) and read (b):

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: What section is the minister reading?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act.
3. (1) If any person for any purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state,
(b)	makes any sketch, plan, model or note which is calculated to be or might be or is intended to be directly or indirectly useful to a foreign power; or
(c)	obtains, collects, records, or publishes, . . . any sketch, plan, model, article, or note, or other document or information-

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: "Or other document or information"-those are surely the important words.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Yes.
-which is calculated to be or might be or is intended to be directly or indirectly useful to a foreign power; he shall be guilty of an offence under this act.
Then follows subsection 2 which the hon. member quoted. It reads:
(2) On a prosecution under this section, it shall not be necessary to show that the accused person was guilty of any particular act tending to show a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state, and, notwithstanding that no such act is proved against him, he may be convicted if, from the circumstances of the case, or his conduct, or his known character as proved, it appears that his purpose was a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state . . .
Official Secrets Act
Keeping that in mind, I should like my hon. friend to look at the new section 12A to be enacted by the bill. It reads this way:
12A. The acts, omissions and things made offences by this act shall be triable and punishable in Canada notwithstanding they were committed outside Canada, in the following cases;
(b) where any code word, pass word, sketch, plan, model, article, note, document, information or other thing whatsoever in respect of which an offender is charged was obtained by him, or depends upon information which he obtained, while owing allegiance to His Majesty in right of Canada.
I suggest that the new section 12A applies quite clearly to the offence of obtaining and passing on this information to which my hon. friend referred. If a Canadian or someone owing allegiance to Canada, not necessarily a Canadian citizen at all but a citizen of another country who does not possess diplomatic immunity or of a country which is not at war according to international law, goes away and discloses information he obtained in Canada, then the extraterritorial effect of 12A will apply and he can be convicted, though the offence did not take place within Canadian territory at all. Have I made my point clear?

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, indeed, as far as the
minister has gone, but he has not quite cleared up what I asked further, as to how wide is the effect of those words in subsection 2 which raise a presumption against him. That presumption, as I see it, in the case of persons of known character is that by communicating with the agent of a foreign power he can be presumed to have been giving information prejudicial to the safety and interests of the state. How wide is the effect of those words? Can these known communists now be prosecuted merely for going behind the iron curtain and having been shown there to have communicated with agents of a foreign power, even though you cannot prove what they said or did?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
My hon. friend is as much a
lawyer as I am, and he has paid me a very delicate compliment in asking for my opinion in the matter. I should think it would turn, would it not, on whether or not it appears that his purpose was prejudicial to the safety of the state? In other words, in the case of a man who had gone to Yugoslavia or Russia and given this information, that person would be charged. The prosecution would open its case and would proceed to prove it under the authority of this amendment just as though the offence had been committed in Canada. When it came to the application of subsection 2 of section 3, I should think that section would apply in relation to that offence which had taken place in Russia just as it would apply in the case of an offence

Official Secrets Act
committed in Canada. The purpose of making it extraterritorial is to have the offence triable in Canada although it took place in another country. As far as section 3, subsection 2 is concerned, I take it that is a provision of general application to all prosecutions under the act. I would be interested to know whether my hon. friend agrees with that view.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: I suppose the only way to find out is for the minister now to institute a few prosecutions against some of these people, as I hope he will.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
I am concerned with the
opening words of section 12A, as to whether they go as far as the minister believes and as far as I am sure we would all like to see them go. Those words are:
The acts, omissions and things made offences by this act shall be triable and punishable in Canada notwithstanding they were committed outside Canada, in the following cases-
The argument put forward by the minister has been that at the very least many offences under the act are not offences if they are committed outside Canada. Indeed his argument may go so far as to suggest that none of them are offences unless they are committed within Canada. It seems to me, however, this section does not expressly say that offences, in the cases referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b), if committed outside Canada are offences. It does not say that. We are up against the problem created by the rule of interpretation to which the minister made reference earlier, that legislation has no extraterritorial effect unless it so provides in express terms. No offence will be created under our law if the act is committed outside Canada, unless our legislation expressly provides that such an act becomes an offence. It seems to me these words fall short of saying that acts committed outside Canada become offences.
I draw attention to the fact that it is only the acts, omissions and things that are made offences by the act that become triable and punishable in Canada, but those acts, omissions and things are not offences under the act today. So it seems to me the words "shall be triable and punishable" are not enough. You must create the offence in the acts, omissions and things committed outside Canada. They have to be made an offence before the provision that they may be triable and punishable in Canada has any effect. Therefore as a matter of drafting and interpretation it seems to me we should have here a provision that such acts, omissions and things as are made offences by this act are offences notwithstanding that they may be committed outside Canada in certain cases. Then the provision that they shall be triable and punishable in Canada may follow.
[Mr. Garson.l
I believe the point I am raising now would be bound to be raised by any counsel acting for an individual accused under this section, and I hope we are not going to leave open any door that might make it possible for that point to be argued successfully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Earlier in the afternoon the hon. member for Lake Centre suggested that we should submit the substance of this bill to a committee of lawyers. I am inclined to think we are getting the same result at the moment. It is a very good result, and we are glad to have these suggestions and to treat them seriously. I must say I do not share the views of my hon. friend. It seems to me the Official Secrets Act states very clearly what shall constitute an offence under it. If that offence takes place in Canada it is triable and punishable in Canada. If it happens to take place outside Canada, heretofore it has not been punishable in Canada.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Because it is not an offence under the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
It is still an offence, but it did not take place here. That is where I differ with my hon. friend. However, it would not be hard to meet the view of my hon. friend, as long as in doing so we do not create more difficulty than we solve. I take it that what he wants is a statement something along these lines:	"The acts,
omissions and things made offences by this act, notwithstanding that they were committed outside Canada shall be offences under this act, and shall be triable and punishable in Canada in the following cases," and then go on with the balance of the section. I am quite agreeable to having this section stand so I may check on this point, because one of the purposes we expect to serve in a committee like this is to obtain the benefit of the views of hon. members. I can do that during the dinner recess.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Then may I touch upon a couple of other points which the minister might be good enough to consider as well. In the first place may I ask what is the relationship of this new offence to extradition? Is this going to be an extraditable offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: No, it is not an extraditable offence. If the hon. member was in the chamber when second reading was moved he may remember I said that the difficulty of actually apprehending an accused might not be so great as it would appear. Citizens in a friendly country such as the United States, who are guilty of this sort of conduct, would probably be deported and we would get them in that way. As I understand it, none of these offences under this act are at the present time extraditable.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
I think, so far as possible, an effort should be made to make offences of this kind extraditable. When we see now that there are gaps, which we are trying to close by extending the territorial effect of the legislation, I believe it would add greatly to the effect of the legislation if such offences could be made extraditable by treaty.
The other point I should like to mention relates to the final words in paragraph (b) of section 2 of the bill. They refer to "owing allegiance to His Majesty in right of Canada". I draw to the attention of the minister the fact that the words "in right of Canada" are not necessary because in the interpretation section of the act the point is already taken care of. Section 2, paragraph (a) of the act, provides that "any reference to His Majesty means His Majesty in the right of Canada or of any province". I think, therefore, those last four words are unnecessary.
I just mention also, Mr. Chairman, that it seems to me unnecessarily restrictive to the scope of allegiance to His Majesty to add "in right of Canada". I am not going to take up the time of the house to discuss the difference between allegiance to His Majesty in the right of Canada and allegiance to His Majesty in the right of some of his other dominions or possessions. I think when we are trying to make this statute as effective as possible, serious consideration ought to be given to removing confining or restrictive words such as those in the interpretation section, "in right of Canada or of any province". In other words to deal with those who are subjects of His Majesty as effectively as we can today the act should simply refer to "subjects of His Majesty", whether they are Canadian subjects of His Majesty or subjects of His Majesty in other parts of the commonwealth, because the offences against which we are legislating are just as deserving of condemnation in the case of any other of His Majesty's subjects as in the case of Canadian citizens. I offer that as a suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
I thought when I was listening to my hon. friend that he perhaps was confusing allegiance with citizenship. Is this not the situation? An alien owes allegiance to this country while he is within the country, unless he has diplomatic immunity. What we are considering here is the trial in Canada of, we will say, an alien, who has obtained information while owing allegiance to Canada -that means while he was within Canada- and then has disclosed that information in another country. I do not think it would make much sense if you indicated he was owing allegiance to another country of the
Official Secrets Act
commonwealth because the prosecution is in Canada. He owes allegiance to Canada while he is here. I believe the phrase used in the bill is the proper and apt phrase. I believe it would serve no useful purpose if you said that, while he owes allegiance to, we will say the British commonwealth-

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: It is still allegiance to His Majesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: -while he owes allegiance to His Majesty in the right of Canada-in other words, if he obtains this information while he is in Canada. That is the whole point. He obtained the information while he was in Canada, and then he has gone to another country and disclosed it to that other country. The purpose of this amendment is to enable us to prosecute him in Canada for disclosing information, say in Russia, which he has obtained in Canada while he owed allegiance to Canada. It seems to me therefore that the reference to his owing allegiance to Canada is quite apt.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext: Will the minister say a word about the removal of the fine, which I am rather sorry to see. While I think the fine should not be made an alternative to a prison sentence, it would mean that a man could get off without a fine. I believe it should be left as a possible addition to a prison sentence. While I do not press it as an amendment to this act, I would like to see the fine left in the case of a corporation, because it was contemplated in the act that there would be a provision for a substantial fine in addition to the prison term which may be imposed upon the directors.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA

. . . but such person may, at the election of the attorney general, he prosecuted summarily in the manner provided by part XV of the Criminal Code, and, if so prosecuted, shall be punishable by fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding twelve months, or by both fine and imprisonment.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHILDREN BORN IN CANADA TO DIPLOMATS, CERTIFICATES TO PERSONS LOSING CITIZENSHIP THROUGH MARRIAGE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
when the Canadian Citizenship Act was passed by parliament in the session of 1946,

the principal objective was the creation of a distinctive Canadian citizenship and the establishment of a procedure designed to instil in our new citizens from other lands an appreciation of the responsibilities and the privileges of Canadian citizenship. This change in our concept of citizenship in Canada was received with enthusiasm from many quarters and has continued to receive the active support of individuals and groups of persons across Canada.
However, as in all experiments with something new, our experience of the past three and a half years since the act came into effect on January 1, 1947, has revealed a necessity for clarification of some of the sections, the addition of certain amendments regarding which there has been a considerable public demand, and, in particular, to bring the act in alignment with recent changes that have taken place in the legislation of other countries of the British commonwealth.
Some of the minor changes which are proposed in this bill are definitions of the words "alien" and "foreign"; a definition of "Canadian ship" expanded to include aircraft; and the deletion of the definition of the word "consulate", to provide for registration under the regulations.
A new provision is that which excludes from the status of natural-born Canadian citizens the children born in Canada of parents who are the diplomatic or consular representatives of foreign governments in Canada, or who are employees in the service of these representatives. It is proposed that it would not be appropriate to permit children who come within this category to be designated as Canadians by birth.
A further important change, and one which has received considerable public support, is that which permits women who were British subjects by birth or by naturalization in Canada, and who lost that status by marriage to aliens prior to January 1, 1947, to be admitted to Canadian citizenship by a simple procedure and without regard to the question of residence. We have had many representations on behalf of these women, who, through no fault of their own, became aliens, and are still aliens, although many of them have never resided outside Canada. Under this amendment, their status will be restored with a minimum of delay.
There is also the case of a person born in Canada who, for one reason or another, became naturalized in a foreign country and thus became an alien. Many of these persons have since returned to Canada with the intention of spending the rest of their lives in their native country. It has been represented to us that these native-born persons should not
Canadian Citizenship Act be required to reside five years in Canada and to follow the procedure required of an alien who was not born in Canada, in order to be admitted to Canadian citizenship. It is proposed, by this amendment, to permit persons in this category to apply for citizenship, by a simple procedure, after a residence of one year in Canada.
A new departure in Canadian legislation is the proposed amendment under the terms of which certificates of Canadian citizenship may be granted to adopted or legitimated children if the adopter, or the legally recognized father, is a Canadian citizen.
Some of the countries of the commonwealth, more particularly India and Pakistan, have discarded the term "British subject". Therefore it has been found necessary to amend that part of the existing act which defines the status in Canada of a British subject who has acquired the status of British subject by birth or naturalization under the laws of any country of the commonwealth. The amendment provides for recognition of the term "commonwealth citizen", and, for the purpose of Canadian citizenship laws, gives it the same meaning as "British subject". This change, and the union of Newfoundland with Canada, necessitates several changes in the first schedule of the existing act. Under the amendment, Ireland and Newfoundland have been deleted from the schedule, and Ceylon, India, Pakistan, and Southern Rhodesia have been added.
There has been considerable discussion concerning the status of citizens of Ireland following the establishment of the Irish Republic and its severance from the commonwealth. This matter has been given very serious consideration in view of representations that the citizens of the Irish Republic who are in Canada should not be placed in the category of aliens. Admittedly, it has been difficult to arrive at a formula which would adequately define their status, particularly in view of the fact that Ireland is not a member of the British commonwealth and therefore cannot be included in the first schedule. I think, however, that the solution proposed in this amendment will meet the situation as it will, in effect, give citizens of the Republic of Ireland the same status as that enjoyed by British subjects in Canada.
Part III of the existing act provides for loss of Canadian citizenship. The bill repeals all of part III and substitutes new sections in which most of the former provisions have been retained, with a few exceptions. One of these permits, in the case of a Canadian who deliberately acquires nationality in an enemy country, a discretion that either he

Canadian Citizenship Act be held to his responsibilities as a Canadian citizen, or that he be deprived of such citizenship.
The other changes in the amendment to part III are of a minor nature, such as discretionary powers for the governor in council and the co-ordination of certain provisions.
There are certain clauses in this bill in which it is intended to make it quite clear that the minister has discretionary power to grant certificates of citizenship. In the existing act, there is a degree of uncertainty as to the extent of these powers, and for that reason these amendments have been included in the bill.
Another change in the existing act is one which provides for the validity and the recognition of certificates of naturalization granted under the Naturalization Act, chapter 77, R.S.C., 1906, or under similar earlier statutes, despite any statutory limitations. Because of these limitations, a person naturalized in Canada under the earlier statutes could not be recognized as a British subject, and did not have the status of a Canadian citizen if he was in the country of his origin and, under the laws of that country, was recognized as a citizen. The amendment will remove this limitation.
There is one other matter which I wish, briefly, to bring to your attention. It concerns clause 19 of the bill, under the terms of which it will be possible to continue, under the provisions of the Citizenship Act, proceedings which were commenced under the Naturalization Act. The reason for this amendment arises from the fact that, some months after the Citizenship Act had been in force, the Department of Justice ruled that proceedings which had been commenced under the Naturalization Act, and which had not been completed before the expiration of that act, could not be continued under the Citizenship Act as the objects were not the same. The application of this ruling has created considerable hardship, particularly among persons who had commenced proceedings in 1946. For these reasons, it is desirable that the act be amended to permit these persons to continue proceedings under the Citizenship Act, as though there had been no interruption.
The remainder of the bill is procedural, covering matters of renumeration and coordination. I am satisfied, however, that if this bill is adopted it will result in a definite improvement in, and a distinct clarification of, the Canadian Citizenship Act.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHILDREN BORN IN CANADA TO DIPLOMATS, CERTIFICATES TO PERSONS LOSING CITIZENSHIP THROUGH MARRIAGE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Citizenship Act is one of the most important acts on our statute

books. I believe the twentieth parliament of Canada had no greater accomplishment to its credit than the enactment of that act in the session of 1946. One recalls that the principle of the measure received the warmest support from all parts of the house, and that it was a major piece of legislation.
There have been in these four intervening years no amendments of any substance, and it is inevitable that after a period of four years some amendments should have become necessary in the operation of the act. Some of the amendments which have been indicated tonight by the minister are obvious in their nature and, I think, do not require elaboration.
One may, however, express a measure of regret that a bill of this kind, which is not a short one, and certainly not unimportant, should have been placed before the house on such short notice. Hon. members are now faced with a bill containing twenty-two sections which amend the act in some important respects. They had this bill placed in their hands just at noon today. All members are very busy at the present time between sittings of the house and sittings of many of the committees of the house which are working very hard writing their reports and bringing their deliberations to a close. I must express regret that an important measure of this kind is brought to us so late in the session, and that the house is asked to take it up on such short notice, which effectively precludes that careful study which a measure of its importance ought to receive. I think it is a measure which might very properly have been referred to the standing committee on external affairs, where its provisions could have been closely examined.
The comments one might feel disposed to make concerning the provisions of the bill may be more properly made in committee of the whole, because they relate to particular sections. It is very difficult to find a principle in a bill like this which one can discuss on second reading, because there are so many amendments which, for the most part, are not related to one another. I think, however, that some very good evidence will be necessary to establish the necessity for the additional ministerial discretion provided in these amendments and the added scope for the regulations, rather than having these matters dealt with by direct enactments of parliament.
There is one thing that perhaps calls for special observation, particularly by those members of this house who have Irish blood in their veins, of whom I am one. I am sure that it would have been a matter of profound regret on the part of hon. members of this house had a decision been made to consider citizens of Ireland as foreigners.

Notwithstanding the fact that the Republic of Ireland has severed ties with the commonwealth I am sure we all welcome the maintenance of brotherly relations with Irishmen, no matter from what part of the lovely green isle they may come.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHILDREN BORN IN CANADA TO DIPLOMATS, CERTIFICATES TO PERSONS LOSING CITIZENSHIP THROUGH MARRIAGE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members of the house welcome the amendments contained in this bill. I join with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) in regretting that the bill was not introduced earlier and perhaps referred to the external affairs committee where it could have been discussed fully although there may have been little in the bill requiring prolonged consideration. That may be the excuse that would be offered for the minister and the government bringing the bill down at this time.
This bill indicates the development of our common citizenship in the strange agglomeration of peoples called the commonwealth of nations. There are actually three methods of acquiring Canadian citizenship provided for in this bill. First, there is the recognition of the usual type of citizenship which we call British citizenship; then there is the new commonwealth citizenship which would include Pakistan, India and so on, and then we have the typically Irish sort of citizenship which is quite difficult to understand and define.
However, I think we all welcome the solution that has been found. The minister did not indicate that this is on a reciprocal basis. I do hope that citizens of Canada who reside in the southern part of the emerald isle will be regarded as citizens of that country in the same way as citizens of Eire are regarded as citizens of Canada.
I am glad to see that there has been a removal of some of the disabilities that existed. I note with considerable interest the change that is to be made in the status of the old citizenship certificates, to be found particularly on the prairies. In the homesteading days people in order to prove up their homesteads acquired what they thought was Canadian citizenship in the fullest sense of the word. Then it was found that, because of certain imperial statutes, they really would have to acquire new naturalization papers in order to receive all the benefits of our common British citizenship. I am quite sure that throughout the years there are thousands of people on the prairies who through ignorance have been exercising all the functions of citizenship, such as voting at federal elections and the rest, without having the legal right so to do. I am glad that those disabilities are being removed by this bill.
Canadian Citizenship Act
I am glad also that the status of citizenship for women is to be changed and I think that is a commendable feature of the minister's proposals. I suppose that these amendments are made in the light of the experience of the last few years and they certainly are in the right direction. I imagine the entire house, regardless of where hon. members sit, will welcome this measure and I do not think it will require lengthy discussion to get general approval.

There is one anomalous situation in regard to citizenship that has been often brought to my attention. A Canadian goes to the United States, signs an application for citizenship and gets what are called the first papers. When he gets those papers he takes an oath in which he declares-I am not going to try to give the exact words, but they are somewhat along these lines-that he renounces allegiance to all foreign princes and potentates, and particularly, in the case of a Canadian, to His Majesty King George VI. In other words he renounces his Canadian citizenship when he makes that declaration; but if he returns to Canada, having renounced our citizenship, he does not lose the right to exercise all the privileges and functions of a Canadian citizen. He is not even required to take out any declaration or oath of allegiance here, or to renew in any form his citizenship in this country.

Canadian Citizenship Act
That always struck me as a very anomalous situation. I remember that on one occasion several years ago the point was raised during a general election. A gentleman who was very active in one of the political parties, it does not matter which, who held office in the organization, was challenged with having taken out his first citizenship papers and having taken this oath; and I believe the matter was referred to Ottawa. The reply was that while he had taken that declaration, under our law he was still regarded as a Canadian citizen. Should not a person who has renounced allegiance to this country, which is really what is meant by renouncing allegiance to His Majesty the King, be required to take a declaration when he resumes his allegiance, or in other words his citizenship in this country? subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHILDREN BORN IN CANADA TO DIPLOMATS, CERTIFICATES TO PERSONS LOSING CITIZENSHIP THROUGH MARRIAGE, ETC.
speechtext:
As I indicated in my statement on the motion for second reading, there has been some doubt as to the authority of the minister to exercise his discretion under the existing act, as to whether he may or may not grant a certificate under certain conditions. In order to remove all possible doubt as to the discretion of the minister we are inserting those words in the sections which have been cited by the hon. member for Eglinton.
The position is simply this. At the moment applicants for citizenship go before county judges for examination. In certain cases it is not possible to produce in the ordinary way evidence which may be available to indicate that a person is not fit for Canadian citizenship. Under those circumstances it is felt that the minister is the person who should accept responsibility for refusing citizenship, and that is the reason for the insertion of these words. I must say that in the four or five months I have had to do with this act there have been occasions on which I have felt that persons should not receive Canadian citizenship. Having in mind the responsibility we owe to parliament and to the Canadian people, it was felt proper that someone in the government should accept responsibility for refusing certificates to certain persons who may apply.

speechtext: Then I ask the minister what was the nature of those cases, because while many of the county court judges in the larger cities have to deal with large numbers of applicants, one would not like to think that great care is not being taken by the judges who have jurisdiction in this matter. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the situation is not quite that. Some judges felt that the present act, the one under which we have been acting, does impose upon the minister the final responsibility for granting certificate. They have discharged their duties by merely reporting to the minister the examination held on the various qualifications under the act, that is that the applicant has resided in Canada so long; intended to reside
Canadian Citizenship Act permanently in Canada; had some qualifications in language, and had some general understanding of our institutions, leaving to the minister what the judge considered was in fact the minister's decision to make. The recommendations in themselves are really not recommendations but are reports of, perhaps for lack of a better term, courts of inquiry. That is one group with which we have had to deal, in which the judge does not make what he considers a final recommendation.
The other group concerns those persons who, because of their past activities or perhaps their present activities, having in mind the discussion which took place in this house this afternoon, are not considered to be persons to whom we should extend the advantages and privileges of citizenship. In some courts in the country evidence of that nature is difficult to produce, because in doing so one might easily disclose the information not only on which it is proposed to deal with that particular application but other information which would affect others as well. Under those conditions, in some cases we have felt that we could not do other than deal with it through the minister rather than through the county judge.

that the judges have not been giving their best attention to those cases. It is for the very reason that some judges have felt that the present act still does rest with the minister the decision whether a certificate should be granted. We hope that parliament will, by passing this amendment, provide the discretion in the minister, but at the same time we will seek to have the judges apply the act in a uniform way so that recommendations will come forward as they formerly have under the act, together with any opinions they care to express.

speechtext:
I have a couple of matters that I should like to discuss with the minister for a short time. There are problems that arise out of the union of Newfoundland with Canada, and particularly in regard to the former act known as the naturalization of aliens act of that province. Under that act a number of Chinese citizens of Newfoundland made application for naturalization as far back as 1947. As a matter of fact, I believe there is a member of the minister's staff in this section who at that time was a member of the department we knew as the department of home affairs, and who is able to verify that a number of applications were made at that time.
These applications were completed in the ordinary form, and I submit to the minister they should be recognized as regular applications. What has happened at the present time is this. All these bona fide applications have been disregarded, and these Chinese people have been told that they have to make new applications, a most unfortunate situation. I submit to the minister that he should take these applications into consideration, and not demand that new applications be made.
That is one point. The other one is this. By order in council passed I believe some time last fall it was agreed that all Chinese who had gone to Hong Kong by December 19, and who had relatives in Canada who had made application for citizenship prior to that time, would be permitted to bring the children or wives who were in Hong Kong at that time. Through circumstances over which these people had no control they were one, two or maybe three weeks late, some of them, in fact, only a couple of days. I would ask the minister in these cases, and under the particular section where he has discretion, and where he knows of the bona fides of these applications, to deal with them in the manner that they should be dealt with, bearing in mind that the communists are now controlling China, and that the people over there are undergoing great hardship.

speechtext: This may apply probably largely to Canadians who became United States citizens. Of course there are others as well as citizens who were naturalized in the United States, but it is intended to make the period one year's residence in Canada again, and after that we may give them a certificate of Canadian citizenship.

ernments. Through the citizenship branch we do contribute, as I have already explained on the estimates, to that work. subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like first to deal with certain aspects of section 1 which defines British ship in the following terms:
"British ship" includes a Canadian ship.
I do not quite understand that definition and I am not quite certain why it is included in the section. A British ship is not otherwise defined in the act. We certainly are not extending the definition of British ship as contained in the British merchant shipping act because that could not be done by Canadian legislation. However, I am prepared to admit that such a definition may be needed here and I am anxious to hear why. If it is considered necessary, I suggest that we have in this section a wording similar to that in section 26 of the Canadian Citizenship Act which reads:
A Canadian citizen is a British subject.
The definition here should then read:
A Canadian ship is a British ship.
I make that suggestion at this stage and I hope it will receive the consideration of the committee. This section also defines Canadian

ship and I am pleased to see this amendment being made in the Canada Shipping Act. This definition reads in part:
"Canadian ship" means a ship registered in Canada-
In all modesty I say that I am particularly pleased with this amendment because I believe I was the first member of this house to request some three or four years ago that this change be made. I also suggested this change on other occasions both inside and outside this house. In order to implement this new definition of a Canadian ship the bill amends the act further by repealing subsection 1 of section 3 of the act and substituting a completely new clause therefor. I shall not discuss that amendment at this stage but will reserve my comments until the appropriate moment.
I make that comment to stress my contention that the clause presently under consideration should contain an additional subsection which probably would appear immediately following subsection 16 and which would amend the definition of registrar as presently defined in the act. The definition of registrar, is to be found in section 2, subsection 81 which reads:	"Registrar means
registrar of British ships." There should be a further amendment to this section to bring it in line with the amendments we are making and to make it read: Registrar means a registrar of Canadian ships. I ask that consideration be given to that suggestion.
This section also amends the definition of foreign ships, the amendment reading:
"Foreign ship" means a ship other than a British ship.
Here again I must confess that I fail to see any reason for this new definition. If the definition is meant to serve a particular purpose, that purpose should be stated clearly. If possible, it should be restricted to the object we have in mind. I expect some clarification of this point from the minister and ask that ctuc. consideration be given to the comments I have made in this respect. Those are all the remarks of a special nature that I wish to make in connection with this section.
I should like to deal now generally with the implications of the amendments contained in this section and the sections immediately following. As I said a while ago, the definition of Canadian ship is provided for in this bill and I consider that a step in the right direction. But I regret that our Canadian ships are not being protected against foreign competition in our coastal trade. This is of great concern to our shipping and shipbuilding industry. The fact is that our ships are discriminated against in certain ways to the advantage of ships of

other nations which are engaged in the Canadian coastal trade. Let us review for a moment the present position of Canadian ships so far as Canada's coasting trade is concerned. At the present time our coasting trade is governed by part XIII of the Canada Shipping Act comprising sections 661 to 665 inclusive. Section 663 reads:
663. (1) No goods shall be transported by water or by land and water, from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, either directly or by way of a foreign port, or for any part of the transportation in any ship other than a British ship.
A similar provision has been made with respect to the transportation of passengers, and penalties are provided for the contravention of these provisions. It is further provided that no foreign-built British ship, regardless of where she is registered, is entitled to engage in the coasting trade of Canada without a licence obtained from the Minister of National Revenue. Exception is made, however, with respect to certain foreign-built vessels which were condemned as prizes of war, or ceded by enemy states to Great Britain or British nationals by the reparations commission during or after the 1914-1918 war. Similar provisions were made with respect to reparation vessels ceded to Canada after the last war.
In order for foreign-built British vessels to obtain a licence from the Minister of National Revenue it is necessary that a duty be paid of 25 per cent ad valorem on the fair market value of hull, machinery, furniture and appurtenances of such vessels. Section 665 provides that exceptions may be made to the foregoing by the governor in council. It is the custom of the Department of National Revenue to issue coasting licences to British ships, other than those which are foreign built, upon submission to that department of proof that the ships are entitled to operate in the coasting trade of Canada, and upon execution by the master and two others, usually officers of the company operating the vessel, of a coasting bond in the amount of $500 in accordance with form D-ll.
The requirements to be fulfilled to obtain a coasting licence, in addition to the filing of the said bond, are as follows:
(1)	Establishing that the ship was British built, that is, built in some part of the British commonwealth of nations, or that it comes within the description of the special exceptions referred to above.
(2)	Production of a certificate of British registry to establish that she is a British ship, that is, registered in some part of the British commonwealth and wholly owned by British subjects.
Canada Shipping Act
(3)	That her officers are properly certificated with British certificates of competency.
A coasting licence is not always required in order to operate in the coasting trade of Canada, but it is a convenience in order that the various requirements will not have to be established to the satisfaction of the collector of customs in each port from which the vessel may clear. The coasting bond requires compliance with the "coasting regulations of this dominion" but no such regulations have ever been issued to my knowledge.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to making three speeches if necessary. I could separate my speech into three parts so that they would apply directly to clauses under study, but I think I am saving the time of the committee by dealing with them together at this stage. Then I will not have to come back to the same subject later on. I think the definition of "Canadian ship" has a definite bearing on the coastal trade and also the definition of "British ship". It is of great moment when we are considering the coastal trade of Canada. As I said a while ago, these are merely preliminary remarks, I shall be through with them in a few moments and then I will deal with the clause under consideration.
If I may be permitted to carry on, Mr. Chairman, in addition it is provided in section 65 of the Customs Act that equipment purchased or supplied or repairs made in a foreign country upon a vessel intended to be employed, or which is later employed, in the coasting trade of Canada, are dutiable if the vessel arrives in Canada within one year of the time such equipment is purchased or such repairs are carried out. The duty with respect to such repairs is 25 per cent ad valorem of the expenses of the repairs, and with respect to equipment it is the same duty as would be charged if such equipment had been imported into Canada in the ordinary course. The words "foreign country" mean any country other than Canada, whether or not such other country is within the British commonwealth of nations. This is my own interpretation, but I have been informed that this interpretation is not accepted by the Department of National Revenue. In the opinion of the department the expression "foreign country" does not include the countries of the British commonwealth of nations. It appears there is no legal basis for such an interpretation, but merely the practice of the department. It is my submission that the expression "foreign country" should include the other countries of the commonwealth, and steps should be taken to bring this about, either by changing the departmental practice in this regard or by defining the expression so there would be no possibility of misinterpretation.
With respect to the meaning of the words "foreign country" as used in the Customs Act, I refer the committee to the case of Cashin v. The King, 35, 4 D.L.R., 547, and particularly the following comment of Judge Angers at page 555:
I think that, for customs purposes, a vessel which is not registered in a Canadian port, even though a British vessel, must be considered a foreign vessel.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of the interpretation of this expression, not only to Canadian ship owners who are

menaced by competition from British vessels, but also to Canadian shipyards and suppliers who would normally carry out the repairs and supply the equipment to vessels operating in the coastal trade of Canada. Indeed, to my mind it would be ridiculous that a Canadian or British ship owner could have his ship repaired in Great Britain or elsewhere within the British commonwealth and come to Canada to engage in the coastal trade without paying any duty on such repairs, though the ship might have all kinds of equipment obtained at lower cost in Great Britain or elsewhere in the commonwealth, whereas if that ship were repaired and equipped in Canadian yards with Canadian labour, using parts, equipment or machinery which had to be imported into Canada from those countries of the commonwealth, such machinery and equipment would be subject to the duty as set out in the tariff; if on the other hand the expression "foreign country" were construed as excluding the other nations of the commonwealth, this would be the logical result.
Similarly, Mr. Chairman, section 66 of the Customs Act provides that surplus stores of vessels arriving in Canada shall be subject to the same duties and regulations as if imported as merchandise. However, if the owner or master desires, to put these stores in warehouse for future use on his vessel, the collector may permit him to do so. At the present time not only British vessels registered in Canada but all British vessels, no matter where they are registered or how they are manned, are given the same opportunity to participate in the coasting trade of Canada, with the proviso that if such vessels, whether registered in Canada or in any other part of the British commonwealth, are not British built, they must first obtain a licence from the Minister of National Revenue, upon payment of duty of 25 per cent.
If vessels registered in Canada could compete economically with vessels registered in Great Britain or other parts of the commonwealth, it might be argued that no restriction should be placed on British ships, which are not registered in Canada, operating in the coasting trade of this country, though even under those conditions many countries afford protection to their own vessels in their coastal trade in much the same way that air line companies of one country are seldom if ever permitted to carry passengers or air cargo from one place to another in a foreign country. However, the situation with respect to coastal shipping is even more serious than this. The costs of operating vessels registered in Canada, with Canadian

wages and under Canadian working conditions, and with repairs and overhauls carried out in Canadian shipyards and with Canadian labour, are -'substantially higher than the costs of operating vessels registered in other parts of the commonwealth, and in particular in Britain. The Canadian maritime commission has given a great deal of study to these comparative costs, and I do not feel it necessary to go into further details concerning this condition.
The competitive advantage of vessels registered in the United Kingdom and other parts of the commonwealth has been further accentuated by the devaluation of sterling and allied currencies within the last year. From the point of view of Canada this problem has been aggravated through the union of Newfoundland and Canada. The trade between Newfoundland and the remainder of Canada, which heretofore has been serviced by vessels registered in Canada, is now menaced by the incursion of British vessels registered in the United Kingdom. It is obvious that if British vessels are permitted to operate in the Canadian coasting trade they will be able to drive out any competition from vessels registered in Canada, since they can be profitably operated on revenues which would not cover the operating expenses of a vessel registered in Canada.
An example of such competition was brought to my attention quite recently, when a Canadian company chartering British-registered ships decided to operate in the Newfoundland trade and sent out a circular letter to prospective clients which in part read:
We are not quite ready to quote any rates, but rest assured that they will be lower than any competing services.
I had a further example of this quite recently also when I was informed that tenders had been called to carry iron ore from Havre St. Pierre to Sorel, and that the rates quoted by the owners of British-registered ships were as much as fifty per cent lower than those quoted by Canadian-operated and Canadian-owned ships.
Canada has faced a great problem in connection with her deep sea shipping, and government policy in this regard was announced by the Prime Minister in a statement in the House of Commons on December 9, 1949. Only a small portion of the present Canadian deep sea fleet will be maintained in operation during the coming year, and a subsidy of $3 million is being provided for this purpose, as it is recognized that without this assistance Canadian vessels could not compete successfully and continue to engage in international trade. Arrangements have been made for 55946-255

Canada Shipping Act the remainder of the deep sea vessels to be transferred to registry in the United Kingdom, and operated under conditions prevailing there. It is obvious that unless Canadian shipping, that is ships registered in Canada and operated under Canadian conditions, are given protection against competition from vessels of other nations, including vessels registered in the United Kingdom and other ports of the commonwealth, such Canadian vessels will be in the same position in the coasting trade of Canada as other Canadian vessels now find themselves in the international or deep sea trade. Ships registered in Canada may find themselves competing-I ask the committee to pay attention to this sentence-with ships now being transferred from Canadian to British registry. It is also feared that competition may be expected from oceangoing British vessels picking up cargoes in the maritimes when proceeding inbound in ballast or with a partial cargo bound for Quebec and Montreal, and often at what might be termed "sacrifice rates". With the development which is expected to take place within the next three years on the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, as well as the development of the St. Lawrence seaway, further opportunities for competition from vessels registered in the United Kingdom and other parts of the commonwealth may be anticipated.
If Canada is to retain any merchant fleet and any body of men capable of maintaining these vessels in time of emergency, it is necessary that protection be given to the operation of vessels registered in Canada in its coasting trade, particularly in view of the decline of Canada's deep sea fleet. It is not only the vessels which are maintained in operation in the coastal trade or even the trained men who man them and who would form a nucleus for expansion in time of emergency who have to be considered, but also the shipyard workers whose services are required in repairing and maintaining these vessels in good condition. It is my submission that it is necessary to take action immediately to protect Canadian vessels and Canadian operators from competition which they will otherwise be unable to meet.
The British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement, which was entered into between the governments of the various parts of the British commonwealth, does not permit immediate restriction of the coastal trade of Canada to vessels registered in Canada or to our newly-born "Canadian ship." One year's notice is necessary in order to change any of the provisions of this agreement. This agreement, and particularly the provisions relating to the right of vessels registered in any part
403S

Canada Shipping Act
of the commonwealth to operate in the coasting trade of any other part on the same terms as ships registered in such part, are entirely favourable to the United Kingdom and possibly to some of the parts of the commonwealth, and are and have been of no benefit to Canada. On the contrary, for the reasons submitted before, they are a serious detriment to Canada. It is recognized that vessels registered in Canada could never compete with vessels registered in the United Kingdom in the coasting trade of Great Britain. It is noteworthy also that the United Kingdom permits not only British vessels registered in other parts of the commonwealth but also foreign vessels to operate in its coasting trade. I understand, however, that the British government has been seriously concerned of late by competition British vessels receive in the coasting trade from Norwegian and other foreign vessels, and is considering restricting its coasting trade, although probably such restriction will be merely to British ships. This is true notwithstanding the fact that British operating costs can be favourably compared to Norwegian costs.
It is realized that there will be certain vessels registered in Great Britain which are now and have been for some years operating in Canada's coastal trade, and that it might be inadvisable to prevent such vessels from continuing to engage in our coasting trade without adequate warning. Exceptions to the policy I am recommending might be made for limited periods with respect to these vessels, particularly if it is found that there are no other vessels registered in Canada which are in a position to carry out the service being performed by such British vessels.
In order to solve this urgent problem, there are two steps which this parliament might take. The first is that notice be given to the signatories of the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement that it is the intention of Canada to change its coasting laws so that the coasting trade of Canada will be further restricted to vessels registered in Canada, owned, manned and operated by Canadians, and that this change will be made on the expiry of one year from the date of the notice. This is the ideal way of solving the problem, but I know that there have been serious objections made to this plan for dealing with the situation, and I understand those objections.
But, Mr. Chairman, there is another way open to us. The following action should be taken immediately, and this is in conformity with the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement: First, we should promulgate coasting regulations applicable to all

vessels operating in the coasting trade of Canada, providing that such regulations applied equally to vessels registered in Canada as to vessels registered in other parts of the British commonwealth. This would not abrogate the provisions of article 11 of the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement. Article 11 especially provides that each part of the British commonwealth may regulate its own coasting trade, but that any such law or regulations shall treat all vessels registered in the British commonwealth in the same manner. It is suggested that these regulations should include the following:
1.	Vessels operating in the coastal trade of Canada should be required to maintain certain standards of wages and working conditions. It might be undesirable to set forth the actual wages and working conditions which should apply, so in this event I would suggest that perhaps the following or some similar phraseology be adopted. All officers and men or other persons employed on vessels engaging in the coasting trade of Canada shall be paid, in legal currency of Canada, such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent employees in the district in which said trade is being carried out for the character or class of work in which they are respectively engaged.
2.	All officers manning a vessel engaged or about to engage in the Canadian coasting trade should be properly qualified to carry out the coasting service. The coasting regulations could provide that any holder of a Canadian coasting, home trade or inland water certificate, would be assumed to be properly qualified for voyages to which their certificates apply.
Since under the Canada Shipping Act the holder of each grade of certificate is entitled to all the rights and privileges of holders of certificates of lower grades, the holders of foreign-going certificates would also be accepted as properly qualified for the coasting trade of Canada, whether on home trade or inland water voyages. However, holders of certificates issued in other parts of the British commonwealth should be required to establish to the administrative authority that they are properly qualified to engage in the coasting trade of Canada, and, for this purpose, to submit to either an oral or written examination. It might be assumed that engineer officers holding proper certificates of competency issued in other parts of the British commonwealth are properly qualified to act in such capacity in the coasting trade of Canada but it is quite reasonable that deck

officers, who have a general qualification certificate to proceed on international voyages, may not have the required local knowledge to ensure the safety of a vessel, including her passengers, crew and cargo, operating, for example, in the coastal waters of Newfoundland or of the St. Lawrence river. Such regulations and requirements were anticipated and are permitted under article 17 of the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement, which reads as follows:
Article 17-Subject to any special provisions that may be made by any part of the commonwealth as to the qualifications to be required of officers on ships engaged in its coasting trade, a valid ''certificate of competency or service granted by one part of the commonwealth will be recognized throughout the British commonwealth as indicating that the holder is duly qualified accordingly when serving on board any ship registered in that part."
3.	Before any ship is allowed to engage in the coasting trade of Canada, the owners of the vessel should be required to satisfy the administrative authority that they have sufficient assets in Canada to reimburse His Majesty the King in right of Canada for any expenses incurred by His Majesty the King in right of Canada in connection with such ship, her master or a member of her crew. With respect to ships registered in Canada, such assets must be disclosed to the registrar of shipping at the time of registration or else security in the form of cash or government bonds or the bond of a recognized surety company must be deposited with the registrar, prior to the registration of such ship. This is in accordance with section 21 of the Canada Shipping Act. The declaration to the registrar or the security deposited with the registrar by the owners of vessels registered in Canada under section 21 of the Canada Shipping Act could be accepted as compliance with this requirement of the coasting regulations. The amount of security required according to the present departmental practice is one dollar for each ton of the vessel's gross tonnage and $50 for each member of her crew, including the master of the ship. It is reasonable that vessels not registered in Canada should be required to provide this security since His Majesty the King in right of Canada may be exposed to expenses with regard to such vessels when operating in the coasting trade of Canada regardless of where the vessels happened to be registered. Amongst those expenses which are contemplated are the expenses which may be incurred in respect of raising or destroying a ship which has foundered and forms an obstruction to a navigable channel.
The fourth action which could be taken in regard to these coasting regulations is that the owners of any vessel applying for a
55946-255$
Canada Shipping Act
coasting licence should be required to establish compliance with section 65 of the Customs Act and should be required to produce an affidavit to the effect that no such repairs or equipment have been received by the vessel within the year prior to arriving in Canada or else give the details of such expenses of repairs and equipment together with proof that the duty provided for in section 65 has been paid. They should also establish compliance with section 66 of the Customs Act.
5. The obtaining of a coasting licence should be made mandatory instead of being merely a matter of convenience and no clearance should be given to a vessel on a coasting voyage unless such coasting licence is produced.
It is further suggested that the administration of the coasting regulations and the authority to grant coasting licences should be taken from the Department of National Revenue and placed under the Canadian maritime commission, so that there will be uniformity in the administration of the coasting regulations and the issuance of the coasting licences. No coasting licence, of course, would be issued unless the issuing authority was satisfied that all requirements, including compliance with the coasting regulations, had been fulfilled.
Provision might be made in the regulations to authorize exceptions to the above regulations with respect to vessels which are now and have been for some years operating in the coasting trade of Canada, when it is found that there are no other vessels which can comply with the regulations, which are in a position to carry out the service being performed by such vessels. No exemptions should be granted for more than twelve months, but applications might be made for renewal.
Before closing my remarks I wish to add that these recommendations have been carried out by other countries of the British commonwealth which were signatories to this merchant shipping agreement, and to my knowledge these countries have remained as good and as faithful members of the British commonwealth of nations as we can ever expect to be able to claim ourselves to be. The countries which have passed similar coasting regulations are Australia and New Zealand. In a news-letter which was sent recently to all members of the house by the Canadian Shipbuilders Association entitled "The Antipodes Show us a Way" we were given the history of these regulations. For example, Australia's navigation act, which is the counterpart of the Canada Shipping Act, for years has given its ministry discretion to restrict the trade to vessels paying crew

Canada Shipping Act
wages at current Australian rates and providing standard accommodation. In New Zealand, the Shipping and Seamen Act has a similar proviso on wage rates and manning scales. That means the home ships get the business.
And just last year, Australia has gone one step further to protect its shipbuilding industry. By the Shipping Act, 1949, coastal licences are reserved to ships less than twenty-four years old at the date of application and built in Australian shipyards or were, at any time prior to the passage of that legislation, engaged in trade exclusively between places in the Commonwealth of Australia.

Mr. Chairman, when this bill was before the house for second reading I made a few remarks. Since then we have had the opportunity of considering it in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Therefore I have no intention of going into detail on the first section of the bill. I do hope to say a few words about the plan to license outboard motors, and also with regard to the need for having radiotelegraph on our coastal ships. However that can be done when we reach those sections.
On this first section I should like to say that I believe the international convention for the safety of life at sea should be accepted by Canada. It stands as a schedule to the

bill, and I do not believe there can be any doubt that Canada would derive great benefits by accepting that convention. I believe it is the intention of the government to do so, and to have the convention formally approved before the end of the present session.
The Canada Shipping Act is a very important statute, and a very long one. There are not many members in the House of Commons who have reason to take much interest in the working out of this act. In fact, even for those of us who live in the coastal ridings the act is somewhat of a mystery. We did not have a very good opportunity in committee to consider the amending bill. At this stage of the session it is difficult for a committee to go into detail in dealing with any question. I wish the bill had been dealt with at a much earlier stage in the session, so that it could have been given more careful consideration. However, that is now water over the dam. I do suggest to the minister, however, that some arrangement be made in his department to go over the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act carefully, and that he allow it to be amended more readily in the future than has been done in the past.
There was an amendment in 1948, and I believe the only amendment before that was in 1938; the original act was passed in 1934. So far as I know there have been no other amendments, so that the act has not been given a great deal of consideration by parliament. It is of much too great importance to be treated in that way. Careful consideration should be given to it, and I hope that the minister and his department will review all the suggestions which came out during the discussion in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and that it may be possible to bring in any amendments during the next session at a much earlier stage so that they may be dealt with more adequately.
